title: Game Swingers Baramulla Win Arni Maal as Kashmir Girls Take the Cricket Field
excerpt: Eight teams from six districts played a four-day knockout tournament in Pattan, organised by the Koshur Foundation. Baramulla beat Bandipora's Kashmir Knights by seven wickets in the final.
body:
• Eight girls' teams from six districts of Kashmir competed in Arni Maal, a four-day knockout cricket tournament at the Pattan Higher Secondary School ground in Baramulla district.
  • Game Swingers Baramulla won the title, beating Kashmir Knights Women's Cricket Club of Bandipora by seven wickets in the final.
  • The tournament was organised by the Koshur Foundation, whose president, Manzoor Ahmad Mir, said the idea came from watching young girls practising cricket locally — and aimed to give them an equal platform in a male-dominated sport.

Girls' cricket in Kashmir has a new landmark: an eight-team, four-day knockout tournament in Pattan that drew players from six districts and finished with Game Swingers Baramulla lifting the trophy.

The Arni Maal tournament, organised by the Koshur Foundation, was played at the cricket ground of Pattan Higher Secondary School in Baramulla district. The eight teams were Game Swingers (Baramulla), Srinagar Knights (Srinagar), Uri Chinar Women's Cricket Club (Uri), Youngsters (Khawaja Bagh, Baramulla), Kashmir Knights Women's Cricket Club (Bandipora), Pulwama Strikers (Pulwama), Sopore Warriors (Sopore) and Budgam Strikers (Soibug, Budgam), according to the foundation's tournament listing.

The final

In the final, Game Swingers Baramulla beat Kashmir Knights Women's Cricket Club, Bandipora, by seven wickets to take the title, according to tournament reports. A seven-wicket margin in a knockout final is a commanding one — the champions chased their target with three wickets' worth of batting still unused and the match under control.

"Cricket has long been a male-dominated sport, so we aimed to provide these girls with an equal platform."

— Manzoor Ahmad Mir, President, Koshur Foundation

Why the organisers built it

Manzoor Ahmad Mir, the Koshur Foundation's president and the tournament's organiser, said the idea came about when he saw young girls practising cricket in the area. The response, he said, was tremendous — around eight teams from six districts, including Pulwama, Uri, Bandipora and Budgam, took part in the four-day knockout event. The foundation framed the tournament around women's empowerment, youth engagement and building a sports culture in the Valley.

What it adds up to

A single community tournament does not change the structure of women's cricket in Kashmir on its own. But district-versus-district competition, with named clubs travelling from Uri to Pulwama to play, is the layer of the game that has historically been missing for girls in the Valley: regular, organised matches outside their own villages. Arni Maal's second edition — if the foundation runs one — will show whether this year's eight teams become a standing circuit.
